definition.text: A measure of how many positively charged ions (cations) a soil can hold on the surfaces of its particles.

facts.text: Negative charges on soil particle surfaces bind cations but let them swap with other cations in the surrounding soil water.
It is the exchangeable positive charge per mass of soil, usually given in cmolc/kg; older texts use the equivalent me/100g or meq/100g.
Because it counts charge, a CEC of 10 cmolc/kg could hold 10 cmol of singly charged Na+ per kilogram of soil but only 5 cmol of doubly charged Ca2+.
Most of it comes from negative charges on clay minerals and soil organic matter, so CEC is usually highest near the surface, where organic matter is richest, and falls with depth.

CEC is used as a measure of soil fertility, showing how well a soil keeps nutrients such as K+, NH4+ and Ca2+ in plant-available form; it also shows its capacity to hold pollutant cations such as Pb2+.
Average CEC at pH 7 for US soils runs from 3.5 cmolc/kg in Ultisols through 18.7 in Mollisols and 35.6 in Vertisols to 128 in Histosols.
A soil's CEC depends on its parent material and the conditions it formed under; the same factors set its pH, which has a major influence on CEC.
Clay and humus are scarce in hot, wet climates because of fast leaching and decomposition, which explains the apparent infertility of tropical soils.

title: Cation exchange

definition.text: The attraction and release of positively charged ions by negatively charged sites on soil colloids, which swap them with ions in the soil water.

facts.text: It is one case of ion exchange, a reversible swap of like-charged ions between an insoluble solid and the surrounding solution; natural exchangers include zeolites, montmorillonite, clay and soil humus.
Exchange between colloids and soil water buffers soil pH, alters soil structure and cleans percolating water by adsorbing both useful and harmful cations.
Held cations keep a shell of water and form no direct chemical bond with the surface, so the hold is weak and other cations from solution displace them easily.
Cations differ in how strongly they are held: at equal amounts Al3+ replaces H+, which replaces Ca2+, then Mg2+, then K+ and NH4+, then Na+.
A cation added in large amounts, as in potash or lime, can displace the others by sheer numbers, an effect called the law of mass action.
As soil water turns more acidic, hydrogen ions take over exchange sites and push weakly held cations into solution, where plants can use them but they can also be leached.
Roots release H+ by making organic acids, lowering the pH next to the root and freeing cations from colloids for uptake.
Held cations resist being washed downward, which preserves soil fertility in areas of moderate rainfall and low temperatures.

notes: Gap-fill: article set to the general Ion exchange page (Cation exchange redirects to Cation-exchange capacity); kept apart from the CEC entry as the process rather than the measure.

title: Permanent charge

definition.text: Negative charge built into a clay's crystal structure where lower-charged atoms replace higher-charged ones; it does not change with pH.

facts.text: Phyllosilicate clays are layered sheets of aluminium and silicon oxides; replacing, for example, Al3+ with Mg2+ leaves the structure with a net negative charge.
This isomorphous substitution happens while the clay forms and does not change with time.
No hydrogen ions are released, so the charge is independent of pH, unlike the variable charges of clay edges and humus.
Kaolinite has almost no isomorphous substitution and so a low CEC, while montmorillonite owes its CEC to magnesium substituting for aluminium.

notes: No article of its own; named on Cation-exchange capacity, Soil and Soil matrix. The clay-minerals chapter may draft isomorphous substitution; merge if so.

definition.text: Surface charge on clay edges and organic matter that changes with the pH of the soil solution, because it comes from hydroxyl groups giving up hydrogen ions.

facts.text: The edges of clay sheets expose many acidic hydroxyl groups that lose their hydrogen at the pH of many soils, leaving negative charges.
Organic matter adds a large share of cation exchange through its many charged functional groups, and its CEC is highly pH-dependent.
Raising the pH, that is lowering the H+ concentration, increases the variable charge and so the cation-exchange capacity.
Hydrogens of humus hydroxyl groups can ionise into solution just as those of clay do, leaving an oxygen with a negative charge.

title: Diffuse double layer

definition.text: Two parallel layers of charge around a particle in a fluid: the surface charge itself and a loosely held diffuse layer of attracted ions that screens it.

facts.text: Exchangeable cations sit in the diffuse layer, held by electric attraction but kept moving by thermal motion, rather than bonding to the surface.
Double layers matter most where surface area is large relative to volume, as in colloids; clay platelets are always surrounded by one.
The layer thins as the electrolyte concentration rises, so adding salt to a suspension shrinks it and destabilises the colloid.
In alkali soils, abundant Na+ crowds into the double layer of clay particles and displaces Ca2+, raising the exchangeable sodium percentage.

notes: Gap-fill: article set to Double layer (surface science); soil facts still cite Cation-exchange capacity, Colloid and Alkali soil.

definition.text: Finding a soil's CEC by displacing all its bound cations with a concentrated solution of another cation, then measuring the displaced cations or the added cation retained.

facts.text: Barium (Ba2+) and ammonium (NH4+) are frequently used as exchanger cations, though many other methods exist.
Because CEC depends on pH it is often measured in a buffer at a set pH; this potential CEC misstates the real value when the buffer's pH differs from the soil's.
Effective CEC, measured at the soil's own pH, is closer to the real value but makes comparing soils harder.
Applications of CaCO3 and CaSO4 can lead to an overestimate of CEC.

sources.title: 7.1: Introduction - Geosciences LibreTexts (Introduction to Soil Science Laboratory Manual (Schwyter and Vaughan))

definition.text: The percentage of a soil's cation-exchange capacity occupied by the base cations Ca2+, Mg2+, K+ and Na+.

facts.text: They are called base cations because they are non-acidic, not because they are bases in the usual chemical sense; hydronium, aluminium and iron are the acid-forming cations.
A soil with a CEC of 20 meq, 5 meq of it aluminium and hydronium, has a base saturation of 15 ÷ 20 × 100% = 75%.
It indexes how weathered a soil is and how available its exchangeable cation nutrients are to plants.
Base saturation rises almost in direct proportion to pH.
It is used to work out the lime requirement, which must count the acid cations held on colloids (exchangeable acidity), not only those in the soil water.
Soil classes turn on it: Alfisols have at least 35% base saturation, the more leached Ultisols less than 35%, and Mollisols more than 50%.

verification.evidence: For example, Mollisols are required to have 50 percent or more base saturation within specified depths.

title: Anion-exchange capacity

definition.text: A soil's ability to hold negatively charged ions, such as nitrate and phosphate, on positively charged surfaces and release them later by exchange.

facts.text: Kaolinite, allophane and iron and aluminium oxides often carry positive surface charges; amorphous and sesquioxide clays have the highest AEC, followed by iron oxides.
In most soils CEC far exceeds AEC, but the reverse can happen in highly weathered soils such as ferralsols (oxisols).
Anions are held with strength in the order H2PO4−, SO42−, NO3−, Cl−, and phosphates tend to stay on exchange sites.
Exchangeable anions amount to tenths to a few milliequivalents per 100 g of dry soil.
AEC falls as pH rises, because the extra hydroxyls displace anions from colloids into solution.
Colloids with low cation exchange capacity tend to have some anion exchange capacity; amorphous and sesquioxide clays have the most, followed by iron oxides.
Iron and aluminium hydroxide clays can swap their hydroxide anions for other anions, and phosphates tend to be held at anion exchange sites.
Anions are held with decreasing strength in the order phosphate (H2PO4−), sulfate, nitrate, chloride.

notes: Section of the Soil hub page; the concept sits with Cation-exchange capacity (Charge and nutrient holding). S:ed61ccc9455e says AEC is lower than CEC 'because of the generally higher rate of positively (versus negatively) charged surfaces'; the reasoning looks inverted, so it is not used.

title: Base-richness

definition.text: The level of chemical bases, such as calcium, potassium or magnesium ions, in soil or water.

facts.text: Bases neutralise acids, so base-rich places are neutral or alkaline (pH>7), while acid ones are dominated by organic acids or by aluminium and hydrogen ions.
Ground over limestone and maritime settings is base-rich; ground over sandstone or granite, or fed directly by rainfall (ombrotrophic), is base-poor.
A higher CEC lets a soil hold more base cations, while sandy or low-organic soils have a lower CEC and leach more nutrients.
Base-richness shows no correlation with the availability of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

notes: S:81221aab8c28 says base-richness correlates negatively with pH, which contradicts S:ca5fd1e66b83 (base-rich environments are neutral or alkaline); left out for the verification pass to check.

title: Base-cation saturation ratio

definition.text: A way of interpreting soil tests that balances soil cations to 'ideal' ratios, either between cations such as calcium and magnesium or as shares of the CEC.

facts.text: It contrasts with the sufficiency level of available nutrients (SLAN) used by most university laboratories, which only keeps each plant-available nutrient between deficiency and excess.
William Albrecht, working in Missouri from the late 1930s, set the ideal balance at H 10%, Ca 60 to 75%, Mg 10 to 20%, K 2 to 5%, Na 0.5 to 5.0% and other cations 5%.
F.E. Bear's 1945 bulletin with Prince and Malcolm proposed 65% Ca, 10% Mg, 5% K and 20% H; Neal Kinsey's later book with Charles Walters became the most influential BCSR work.
Reviews in 1916 and 1933 found no evidence that the Ca:Mg ratio affects growth, and later trials saw no yield difference across ratios so long as calcium dominated.
Much of the evidence for BCSR is explained by pH: Albrecht did not control it, and liming frees molybdenum, which legumes need to form root nodules.
A 3-year SARE trial found BCSR fertiliser cost $9.27 per acre more each year with no higher yield.
On low-CEC soils the method can leave crops short of a nutrient, because it sets ratios but no minimum amounts.

contested_note: Supporters claim balanced cation ratios improve crop quality, livestock health and soil biology, while controlled studies find no benefit beyond what pH and deficiency correction explain.
notes: Claims of over a million acres (4,000 km2) in use rest on the page's unsourced lead (S:141c3405b4e2, S:8f5ab8d2c77b).

title: William Albrecht

definition.text: American soil scientist (1888–1974) who chaired the Department of Soils at the University of Missouri and linked soil fertility to human health.

facts.text: From poor forage and ill livestock he derived a formula of ideal soil cation ratios, the base-cation saturation ratio.
He did not discover cation exchange, as is sometimes supposed, but may have been the first to link it with colloidal clay particles.
He discounted soil pH, crediting the benefits of liming to the added calcium; because his studies did not control pH, they give little firm support to BCSR.
He was 1939 President of the Soil Science Society of America; his papers went to Charles Walters, founder of the magazine Acres USA.

notes: Individual scientist outside the founders list, assigned to this chapter by the concept graph; drafted as the originator of BCSR but excluded by the scientist rule.

title: Discovery of cation exchange

definition.text: The 19th-century finding, by Thomas Way and John Bennet Lawes at Rothamsted Experimental Station, that soils exchange cations.

facts.text: J. Thomas Way, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society in England, ran many experiments on how soils exchange ions and is considered the father of soil chemistry.
William Albrecht is sometimes credited with the discovery, but he may only have been the first to link cation exchange with colloidal clay particles.

notes: Named on Base-cation saturation ratio, Soil chemistry and William Albrecht. Soil chemistry (S:199df23b01e4) puts Way's exchange experiments in the early 1870s, while Soil (S:bc95949dbb4e) has Way at work in 1856; the date is worth checking.

definition.text: Dark, relatively decay-resistant organic compounds formed during the long-term decomposition and transformation of biomass residues.

facts.text: They make up most of the organic matter in soil, peat, coal and sediments, and much of the dissolved organic matter in lakes, rivers and sea water.
Humic substances account for 50 – 90% of the cation-exchange capacity of soils.
The term covers three fractions that differ in solubility: humic acid, fulvic acid and humin.
Their colour runs from bright yellow through light or dark brown to black; the name comes from the Latin humus, meaning 'soil, earth'.
They form by microbial breakdown of dead material such as lignin, cellulose and charcoal, yet how they form is among the least understood parts of humus chemistry.
Historic theories of their formation were Waksman's lignin theory (1932), the polyphenol theory and Maillard's sugar-amine condensation theory (1911).
Those from soil and peat, formed over hundreds to thousands of years, have higher molecular weights and more oxygen and nitrogen than those from coal and leonardite, formed over millions.

title: Humic acid

definition.text: The fraction of humic substances that dissolves in water at neutral and alkaline pH but not at acidic pH below 2.

facts.text: Extracted humic acid is a complex mixture of many acids with carboxyl and phenolate groups that behaves as a dibasic, or occasionally tribasic, acid.
Reported number-average molecular weights of soil humic acid are below 6000, though it is highly polydisperse.
Green manure lowers the pH of alkali soils by generating humic acid.
Its potassium salt, potassium humate, is extracted from leonardite and used mainly as a soil conditioner.

notes: No article of its own (redirects to Humic substance); named on Humic substance, Leonardite, Potassium humate, Green manure, Glomalin and Humin.

title: Fulvic acid

definition.text: The fraction of humic substances that dissolves in water at any pH.

facts.text: It has more carboxylic groups and a lower average molecular weight than humic acid, and is more acidic.
Fulvic acids have a higher cation-exchange capacity, interact more strongly with fertilizers and form soluble chelates of trace metals.
Chelates of fulvic acid and metal ions in humus are strongly leached and redeposited, an important part of cheluviation.
Measured number-average molecular weights of aquatic fulvic acid are below 900.

notes: No article of its own; named on Humic substance, Potassium humate, Cheluviation, Colloid and International Humic Substances Society.

definition.text: The laboratory separation of natural organic matter into humic acid, fulvic acid and humin by alkaline extraction and acidification.

facts.text: Soil is extracted with 0.1 M NaOH under nitrogen to prevent oxidation; the organic matter left unextracted is humin.
From natural waters, humic and fulvic acids are caught on a resin column after microfiltration and acidification to pH 2; humic acid is then precipitated at pH 1.
The International Humic Substances Society advocates standard methods, and commercial humic acid for soil amendment is made by these procedures.
The definition of humic substances is thus largely operational, rooted in alkaline extraction that goes back to Franz Karl Achard's treatment of peat with potassium hydroxide in 1786.

title: Chemistry of humic substances

definition.text: The make-up of humic substances: mixtures of many molecules built from aromatic, aliphatic and carbohydrate units that carry mainly carboxylic and phenolic groups.

facts.text: Carboxylic and phenolic groups give most of their surface charge and reactivity, protonating at a pK around 4 and around 8 respectively.
These groups let humic acids form complexes, often chelates, with Mg2+, Ca2+, Fe2+ and Fe3+, which regulates the bioavailability of metal ions.
Mass spectroscopy finds thousands of distinct components, and molecular weights are lower than once thought.
Their molecular structure is still debated: the traditional view sees large poly-condensates associated with clay, a newer one supramolecular associations of small molecules.

contested_note: Sources disagree whether humic substances are large macromolecular poly-condensates or supramolecular associations of relatively small molecules.

title: Humification debate

definition.text: The dispute over whether humic substances exist in soil as distinct compounds or are products of the alkaline extraction used to isolate them.

facts.text: Alkaline extraction, used by soil chemists since the 18th century, led to the theory that a 'humification' process creates distinct humic acid, fulvic acid and humin.
Modern analysis of unprocessed mineral soil has not directly observed large humic molecules, which suggests extraction alters the organic matter.
Because humic and fulvic acids are defined by that separation, it is unclear whether the categories reflect the natural state of soil organic matter.
Some researchers argue that alkali extraction misrepresents humic substances because it uses highly alkaline extracts rather than water.
The humification theory persists, even in textbooks, and attempts to redefine humic substances have produced conflicting definitions that hamper communication.

contested_note: Critics hold that humic substances are artefacts of alkaline extraction, while the humification concept persists in the field and in textbooks.

title: Humic substances and plant growth

definition.text: The effects of humic substances and other soil organic matter on plant growth and soil fertility.

facts.text: Until Liebig showed that plants grow on inorganic compounds, humus was thought to feed plants directly; afterwards organic matter was valued only for the nutrients released as it broke down.
Soil scientists now at least recognise that humus affects fertility through the soil's water-holding capacity.
Plants may absorb soluble forms of humus, perhaps an essential route for taking up otherwise insoluble iron oxides.
Studies found humic acids increased plant growth even at low application rates, and humate added to soil raised root mass in creeping bentgrass turf.

contested_note: The chemistry and function of organic matter in plant growth has been disputed since the 18th century, and direct uptake of humus is still not settled.

definition.text: Humic-like substances produced by people, by composting lignin, adding biochar, or synthesising them industrially from organic feedstocks.

facts.text: Hydrothermal humification turns biomass into artificial humin, humic and fulvic acids at 180 °C–250 °C in an alkaline solution within minutes to hours, against years in nature.
Artificial humic acids have eased the effects of drought on soil microbial communities.
Oxidising lignite also yields humic substances, reversing coal formation; this 'mineral-derived fulvic acid' is widely used in China.
Synthesised humic substances were used to save a 160-year-old beech tree in Park Sanssouci, Potsdam, stressed by water scarcity and sandy soil.

definition.text: In economic geology, rock material rich in humic acids, such as weathered coal beds (leonardite), mudrock or pore material in sandstones.

facts.text: Humate has been mined from the Fruitland Formation of New Mexico as a soil amendment since the 1970s, with nearly 60,000 metric tons produced by 2016.
Humate deposits may also play an important role in forming uranium ore bodies.

title: Humic acid in drinking water
article: Humic substance#Determination of humic acids in water samples

definition.text: Humic acid in water meant for drinking or industry, where it affects how well the water can be treated and disinfected.

facts.text: Humic and fulvic acids react with chlorination chemicals to form disinfection byproducts such as dihaloacetonitriles, which are toxic to humans.
Measuring it matters most for supplies drawn from upland peaty catchments in temperate climates.
Because exact measurement is cumbersome, its concentration is usually estimated from total or dissolved organic carbon.

definition.text: A physical and chemical process by which one substance becomes attached to another.

facts.text: It covers absorption of a substance into another of a different state, adsorption of ions and molecules onto the surface of another phase, and ion exchange.
Rates of adsorption and absorption of a dilute solute onto a surface can be calculated with Fick's laws of diffusion.
Much soil humus persists for over 100 years partly because it is tightly sorbed or complexed to clays, out of reach of microbes and enzymes.
Molybdenum sorption is strongest in acid soils, and liming often relieves molybdenum deficiency by decreasing it.
Aluminium sorbed onto exposed hydroxyl groups gives clay plate edges a slight positive charge, so they stick to the negative faces of other particles and flocculate.
In alkali soils, ammonium from urea, a strongly sorbing cation, exchanges with weakly sorbing Na+, releasing the sodium into water.

definition.text: The bonding of a metal atom by a molecule that grips it at two or more points, forming a ring structure.

facts.text: The binding molecule, or ligand, is called a chelant, chelator, chelating agent or sequestering agent; it is usually, but not necessarily, organic.
The name comes from the Greek chēlē, 'claw', since the ligand holds the metal like a crab's claws; Morgan and Drew first used 'chelate' in 1920.
Most metal complexes in nature are bound in some kind of chelate ring, for example with a humic acid or a protein.
Metal chelates govern the mobilisation of metals in soil and their uptake and accumulation by plants and microorganisms.
Humus, a negatively charged colloid, raises a soil's cation-exchange capacity and so its ability to store nutrients by chelation.
Chelation is used in nutritional supplements, chelation therapy for toxic metals, MRI contrast agents, catalysts, water treatment and fertilizers.
Dechelation reverses it, recovering the chelating agent by acidifying the solution with a mineral acid to form a precipitate.

definition.text: The greater affinity of a chelating ligand for a metal ion than of similar ligands that bind it at only one point.

facts.text: Bidentate ligands bind metal ions to form a chelate ring; as in organic chemistry, 5- and 6-membered rings predominate.
Cadmium holds ethylenediamine, which forms a five-membered ring, far more strongly than two methylamine ligands of about the same donor power.
The enthalpy changes of the two reactions are about equal, so the chelate effect is mainly an effect of entropy.

title: Natural chelating agents

definition.text: Molecules made by living things, such as proteins, polysaccharides, organic acids and microbial siderophores, that bind metal ions as chelates.

facts.text: Organic diacids such as malate, amino acids such as glutamic acid and histidine, and peptides such as phytochelatin are typical natural chelators.
Many microbes secrete water-soluble pigments called siderophores; Pseudomonas species release pyochelin and pyoverdine, which bind iron.
Chemical weathering is attributed to organic chelating agents, such as peptides and sugars, that extract metal ions from minerals and rocks.
Plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria produce siderophores that chelate iron and make it available to plant roots.

notes: Siderophores have no crawled article but are named on Chelation, Orchid mycorrhiza, Rhizobacteria, Soil mechanics and Weathering; folded in here.

definition.text: Fertilizers that supply micronutrient metals such as manganese, iron, zinc and copper as metal chelate compounds.

facts.text: Without a chelating agent, the phosphate salts in most fertilizers turn these metal ions into insoluble solids of no use to plants.
EDTA is the typical chelating agent that keeps the metals soluble; iron is often given as EDTA or EDDHA chelates.
Chelating a foliar-applied nutrient improves its absorption and movement in the plant and avoids losses to soil and groundwater.
Consumption of EDTA and NTA is declining (−6% annually) over toxicity and environmental concerns, as greener chelators such as EDDS and citrate gain ground.

definition.text: A soft, waxy, black or brown mineraloid formed by the oxidation of lignite, which dissolves easily in alkaline solutions.

facts.text: It is a rich source of humic acid (up to 90%), used as a soil conditioner, in water treatment, in the remediation of polluted environments and as a drilling additive.
It occurs with near-surface lignite deposits; first described from North Dakota, it is named after A. G. Leonard, first director of the North Dakota Geological Survey.
It conditions soil either applied directly to the land or as a source of humic acid or potassium humate.
Added to contaminated ground, especially with compost, it reduces the uptake of metals by plants.

definition.text: The potassium salt of humic acid, made by alkaline extraction of leonardite and used mainly as a soil conditioner.

facts.text: It is extracted in water with potassium hydroxide, sequestering agents and surfactants, using heat to raise humic acid solubility, and dried into granules that can be added to fertilizer.
Well-oxidised lignite (leonardite) is the best source: the less oxidised the coal, the less potassium humate it yields, and low-ash sources give the best quality.
It is used as a fertilizer additive to make nitrogen and phosphorus inputs more efficient.

definition.text: The pH at which the net electrical charge on a particle's surface is zero.

facts.text: Below the point of zero charge a surface turns positive and adsorbs anions; above it, the surface is negative and adsorbs cations.
The idea came from studies of colloid flocculation; at this point particles have zero zeta potential and flocculate fastest.
It is usually found by acid–base titration of a colloid suspension while tracking pH and the particles' electrophoretic mobility.
It governs how readily a surface adsorbs harmful ions, and because soil pH sets mineral surface charges it also shifts emissions such as nitrous acid.

definition.text: The adhesion of atoms, ions or molecules from a gas, liquid or solution to a surface.

facts.text: It builds a film of adsorbate on the adsorbent and, unlike absorption, does not penetrate into the bulk of the material.
Sorption covers both adsorption and absorption; desorption is the reverse.
It arises from surface energy: atoms at a surface are not fully surrounded by their neighbours and can attract adsorbates.
Bonding is classed as physisorption, through weak van der Waals forces, or chemisorption, through covalent bonding; electrostatic attraction can also cause it.
Adsorption, ion exchange and chromatography are sorption processes that selectively move adsorbates from a fluid onto insoluble particles.
Physically adsorbed water on solids is removed by drying, while chemically adsorbed water may split into surface -H and -OH groups.
German physicist Heinrich Kayser coined the word in 1881.

definition.text: A description of how much substance is adsorbed on a surface as a function of its pressure, or of its concentration in solution, at constant temperature.

facts.text: The quantity adsorbed is nearly always divided by the adsorbent's mass so materials can be compared.
Freundlich and Kuster published the first, purely empirical fit; Langmuir derived the first scientifically based isotherm.
The Langmuir model assumes equivalent sites holding one molecule each, an energetically uniform surface and at most a monolayer, assumptions seldom all true.
Choosing between Langmuir and Freundlich should rest on adsorption enthalpies, constant in Langmuir and falling with coverage in Freundlich, not on best fit.
The 1938 BET isotherm allows multilayers; Langmuir usually suits chemisorption, BET physisorption on non-microporous surfaces.
The monolayer capacity from a Langmuir fit can be used to calculate the adsorbent's surface area.
Linearized fits are no longer common practice now that nonlinear regression is fast.

conflicts.note: The Adsorption page dates Langmuir's isotherm to 1918 (S:3f112d1357dd); the Langmuir page says 1916.

definition.text: The release of adsorbed atoms or molecules from a surface into the surrounding fluid or vacuum; the reverse of adsorption.

facts.text: It happens when a molecule gains enough energy to overcome the activation barrier and binding energy holding it to the surface.
Heat, light, energetic particle beams or chemical reactions such as oxidation or reduction can drive it.
Thermal desorption is described by the Polanyi–Wigner equation, whose kinetic order links surface coverage to desorption rate.
As remediation, thermal desorption heats contaminated material to 90–560 °C to volatilize water and organic contaminants, which a gas treatment system then collects or destroys.

definition.text: The amount of a substance that reacts with, or is equivalent to, a set amount, typically one mole, of another substance in a reaction.

facts.text: Formally, it is the amount that reacts with or supplies one mole of hydrogen ions in an acid–base reaction, or one mole of electrons in a redox reaction.
The number of equivalents of an ion equals its moles multiplied by its valence.
Thus 1 mmol of Na+ is 1 milliequivalent, but 1 mmol of Ca2+ is 2 milliequivalents.
It is an archaic quantity; small amounts are given in milliequivalents (meq), thousandths of an equivalent.
The sum-of-cations method adds up all the exchangeable cation quantities listed in a soil analysis to give the CEC.

The mineralogy method approximates CEC from the type and amount of each clay mineral; the manual uses 10 cmolc/kg for kaolinite, 100 for montmorillonite/smectite and 150 for vermiculite, though real colloids vary.
A soil with 10% kaolinite clay contributes 10 cmolc/kg clay times 10 kg clay per 100 kg soil, or 1.0 cmolc per kg of soil.

Colloids, below 0.002 mm, are called the active fraction because their charged surfaces are highly reactive; their small size gives large surface area per unit weight and their ionic structure a net charge.

definition.text: CEC can be estimated either by summing the exchangeable cations in a soil analysis or by weighting typical CEC values of the clay minerals present.

facts.text: Saline soils have EC above 4 dS/m but SAR below 13 and ESP below 15%, pH usually under 8.5, and flocculated colloids.
Sodic soils have EC below 4 dS/m but SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%, and pH usually above 8.5 from hydrolysis of Na2CO3.
Saline-sodic soils have EC above 4 dS/m, SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%; their pH is usually below 8.5 and they stay flocculated.
Hydrated Na+ between clay particles cancels the binding electrostatic forces and extra water layers push the particles apart, dispersing sodic soil; high pH also disperses organic matter.
Saline soils are aggregated with high infiltration so they leach easily, but dispersed sodic and saline-sodic soils infiltrate poorly and usually need gypsum.
Calcium replacing monovalent Na+ promotes aggregation and infiltration, and the displaced sodium and salts are leached; saline drainage may be diverted through subsurface drains.
Salt-tolerant crops such as barley or sunflower and trees can take up salts, but prevention is better than reclamation.

Natural sources include mineral weathering, atmospheric deposition, seawater intrusion, saline groundwater and natural brines; human sources include salty irrigation water, salty fertilizers, manure, biosolids, compost and road salt.

definition.text: Salt-affected soils are classed as saline, sodic or saline-sodic by total salt (EC) and sodium content (SAR, ESP).
